NEW DELHI: A petition has been filed in the Supreme Court challenging the appointments of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi.Through the petition, the petitioner has sought a writ of quo warranto against Kumar, Sandhu and Joshi and challenged the validity of their appointments to the Election Commission , according to Live Law report.The plea contends that their appointments did not follow the procedure prescribed under the CEC and other ECs (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.The petitioner has argued that under Section 6 of the Act, a panel of five names should have been prepared for each vacancy before the appointments were made. The plea claims this procedure was not followed.Rhe eligibility of the three officials was also challenged, arguing that none of them had previously handled election-related assignments and therefore did not meet the eligibility requirements under Section 5 of the 2023 Act.The plea also refers to the Supreme Court’s March 2024 proceedings concerning the appointments, where the court had expressed concern over the manner in which the selection process was conducted and said complete details of candidates should be circulated to members of the selection committee.This update comes days after the Supreme Court of India refused to pass an interim order to suspend CEC Gyanesh Kumar, while issuing formal notices to the Centre, the Election Commission of India (ECI), CEC Gyanesh Kumar, and other respondents.
Article Summary: A petition has been filed in the supreme court challenging the appointments of chief election commissioner gyanesh kumar and election commissioners sukhbir singh sandhu and vivek joshi. The plea contends that their appointments did not follow the procedure prescribed under the cec and other ecs (appointment, conditions of service and term of office) act, 2023.

The 1980s was a good decade to grow up in India. Not too far off from Independence, and two decades shy of the 21st century; it was an India that gave children enough room to discover and know themselves before they went out to the big, bad world out there. Mornings were rushed. Afternoons were lazy. Evenings were long and a time to catch up with neighbours from verandahs and terraces. This was also an India where young people had the freedom to play outdoors — though strict rules applied. And when night came, it was full of promise to read our favourite books. And on top of the reading list was Jeffrey Archer.Which is why when the news of his death broke Monday, there was this whole generation — Gen X mostly but Boomers and Millennials too — who were promptly transported to a time when living life used to be a peaceful affair. When parents, grandparents and teachers were all guides who would tell children how to brush up their English-speaking skills. And British author Archer was on top of the list because he knew how to write page-turners in the simplest language.In this India, privilege was education. And going to an English medium school or Bengali medium, where English was the second language was why our parents worked hard. Dads at their workplace, and moms at home helping finish our homework.Even in homes where both parents worked, the setting wasn’t too different. Grandparents bright a lot of us up. The 1980s was a decade and half shy of the nuclear family. There were mini-libraries in every house (read two to three cupboards full of books). There would be a mix of literature — mostly fiction — in our first language and English.In Bengali households, after Bengali literature, it was the Russians who sat pretty and fat in those library cupboards. But then there were easy English fictions. Enid Blyton, Agatha Christie, Sherlock Holmes and Jeffrey Archer. Well, there was also Sydney Sheldon. But we were told those were “adult” books not to be touched till we were 16. But as things go, almost everyone we knew had read all Archers and all Sheldons by 16 years of age.There was something about those books that made them travel easily from one generation to another, and from one house to another. You didn’t have to be a serious reader to pick up a Jeffrey Archer. You didn’t need to know anything about literary criticism or understand what made a novel important. You simply needed to be curious about what happened next. That was Archer's great gift. That’s also essentially how generations of people fell in love with reading.Then came the imagination of what adult worlds look and feel like. As school students in the 1980s India, we knew of worlds far off and very different from ours through fiction. Also, as teenagers, when hormones are running wild, there was this insane urge to know about all kinds of unfelt emotions we watched in movies and read in books — but didn’t fully comprehend ourselves because those worlds seemed far off. But very attractive. And full of tales of people who wanted something badly.Money, power, revenge, love, recognition, another chance at life. There were families, rivalries, fortunes, secrets, political ambitions and people who seemed to have everything until one twist of fate changed it all. The stories were set in worlds that were far removed from the India most of us knew, but the emotions were not. Ambition was ambition. Jealousy was jealousy. A family feud was a family feud. And a person who had lost everything and wanted to start again was a character anyone could understand.That was also why Archer became such an easy entry point into English fiction. The language didn’t stand between you and the story. At a time when many Indian children were learning English as a second language, Archer books became handy. Almost an already-available tool that helped out both parents and teachers.Parents wanted us to read because they believed good English could change our lives. Teachers recommended books because they knew that children who read would eventually write and speak better. And Archer didn't feel like homework. His books were what you read after the homework was done. At times even when mom had asked us to turn off my light. We would turn off the light, say goodbye, listen intently—like a cheetah hunting its prey—to our parents’ steps withdrawing from our rooms. Hold our breaths for 10 minutes, and then promptly turn on the torch inside our sheet covers to read a couple of more chapters.That was the beginning of the relationship between India and Jeffrey Archer. He arrived at the precise moment when books still had enormous power in middle-class homes. There was no internet to tell you what was trending. No Instagram account to follow. No streaming platform recommending the next series. There were just newspapers, magazines, television and books. And books could take you somewhere else for as long as you wanted.An Archer novel was particularly good company on a long afternoon or a long train journey. It could make a railway compartment disappear. It could turn a summer holiday into something you remembered years later. It could keep you awake under the blanket with a torch because you were determined to finish one more chapter and then another. And the next day as one would inevitably fall asleep in the classroom, the teacher would gently pat us awake and ask which book we were reading last night. The whole class would laugh. Then it would be another student’s turn. This was a ritual in 1980s school life.Archer himself knew that no country held him close quite like India. By his own estimation, more than 50 million Indians had read his 1979 masterpiece,. When he toured the Western world, a typical book signing in New York or London might bring in 200 or 300 readers. But when he stepped off the plane in Delhi, Mumbai or Bangalore, he was greeted like a pop star by crowds of 2,000 to 3,000 eager fans. What moved him most was how young these readers were. At a 2013 gathering of 1,000 fans in Bangalore, eight out of ten people in the room were under 20 years old.That tells us about the peculiar place Archer occupied among Indians. He wasn't just a bestselling foreign novelist. He was the author who introduced us to the pleasure of reading for pleasure. He was the book we borrowed from an older cousin, the paperback that travelled through a classroom, the novel somebody recommended with a slightly conspiratorial “You must read this.” He became part of the informal education of a generation.Many of us discovered him in school libraries or through friends, and then went looking for the rest of his books.. Once you had read one, you knew there were more waiting. That excitement is still palpable and was felt by most of us as we heard of the author’s demise.Books were not as easily available back in the day as they are today. Finding another Archer could itself feel like an achievement. At times two people would read it and two different pages would be dog eared. That’s how people read books in those times. It seemed the world would fall apart if the next chapter was not finished by the end of school.Teachers and librarians played their part too. In an India where parents saw English as one of the most important gifts they could give their children, books that were accessible but exciting were invaluable. Archer’s stories offered unfamiliar worlds. But we could dream we would be a part of this world some day. We could read about international banking, political campaigns, art auctions or courtroom battles and still follow the story not just because we saw ourselves as the protagonist but also because the language was simple and clear.A paperback could be finished by one person on Monday and be in somebody else's schoolbag by Tuesday. Pages became dog-eared, covers disappeared, names were written inside them. Books were rarely pristine possessions. They were used, borrowed, exchanged and sometimes never returned.Archer's stories also had something that felt instinctively familiar to Indian readers: a love of drama and fate.is essentially the story of two men born on the same day but into completely different worlds, whose lives become intertwined through ambition and rivalry. William Lowell Kane is born into privilege in Boston, while Abel Rosnovski grows up in poverty and survives extraordinary hardship before building an empire of his own. It is an enormous story, but its emotional core is simple. Two men want to make something of their lives and neither is willing to give way.For an ambitious Indian middle class, particularly the generation that came of age around and after the economic reforms of 1991, there was something irresistible about that. The idea that circumstances did not have to determine your destiny was deeply appealing. Archer’s characters were forever trying to escape the lives they had been given and build better ones.His stories also understood that people were rarely entirely good or entirely bad. They were complicated by family, pride, love, money and circumstance. That too was familiar. Indian storytelling had long been comfortable with characters who could be generous and selfish, noble and flawed, loving and resentful at the same time. In that sense, Archer's worlds, however Western they appeared on the surface, did not feel entirely alien.And then there were the twists. Archer understood the sheer pleasure of making a reader gasp. Separated twins, secret identities, unexpected inheritances, betrayals, reversals of fortune, family ambitions, betrayals — his stories were constantly nudging you towards one conclusion and then taking you somewhere else.took the reader into the world of American politics and a plot to assassinate the President.showed just how much drama could be packed into a short story, with its tales of deception, revenge and unexpected reversals. And, the sequel to, took the saga into another generation, following Florentyna Rosnovski as she rises through American politics and pursues the ambition of becoming the first woman President of the United States.These were stories that could have been written for an Indian movie audience. And Indian filmmakers noticed. It was no surprise that his books found their way into Indian cinema, sometimes with permission and sometimes without it. Rakesh Roshan's 1987 film, starring Jeetendra and Shatrughan Sinha, drew heavily from. The story travelled further through regional cinema, and years laterprovided the inspiration for the trickster plot of Yash Raj Films'Archer was not particularly amused by this. He famously referred to Bollywood as “a bunch of thieves”. But the irony was that the very industry borrowing his stories was also proof of how naturally his storytelling fitted the Indian imagination.But long before streaming platforms discovered him, Archer belonged to another India — one where his books travelled through railway stations and pavement stalls. The extraordinary parallel world of India's street book trade. Pirated copies of popular books could appear almost as quickly as the originals. Archer himself recalled how, within days of a new book being released abroad, copies could find their way to Indian streets. Someone would buy the new edition, fly back to India and the presses would get to work.From 2008 onwards, India became a regular part of Archer’s international tours, and he often seemed to enjoy the enthusiasm here in a way that was quite different from the more restrained response he received elsewhere. He called Indians among the biggest readers in the world and spoke warmly about the country's love of physical books.He had his own affection for India too. RK Narayan was a writer he admired deeply, and he considered him worthy of the Nobel Prize in Literature. Cricket gave him another connection with the country. He became friendly with Indian cricketing greats including Sunil Gavaskar, Kapil Dev, Rahul Dravid, Anil Kumble and Mansur Ali Khan Pataudi. With his usual flair, Archer once called himself the “Sachin Tendulkar of England”.Indian readers wanted even more from him. But Archer didn't have to write an India novel to become part of Indian literary memory. India had already made him its own.That is why his death brings back more than memories of a bestselling author. It brings back an entire reading culture. The book cupboards in our parents' homes. The school libraries. The railway stalls. The borrowed paperbacks. The books we were told were too adult for us and read anyway. The evenings when there was nothing urgent to do and a novel could fill the entire night.For this generation of Indian readers, Archer was never quite a foreign author. He was the writer whose novels moved from one bedroom to another, from one cousin to another, from one schoolbag to another. He was there when many of us were discovering that reading could be more than something you did for school.Archer didn't change the way we read because he was a great literary stylist. He changed it because he made reading irresistible. He understood that a book does not have to teach you anything, improve you or make you more sophisticated. It simply has to make you want to turn the page.For millions of Indians, opening an Archer novel still brings back a particular kind of memory: the smell of platform tea on a train journey, a dog-eared paperback borrowed from a classmate, a book pulled out of a crowded cupboard on a lazy afternoon, or the quiet excitement of staying awake under the covers because there was only one more chapter left.For those who grew up with his books and in those times, saying goodbye to Jeffrey Archer feels a lot like saying goodbye to a part of the India we grew up in and loved dearly. An India we miss sorely in these crazy times.
Article Summary: The 1980s was a good decade to grow up in india. It was an india that gave children enough room to discover and know themselves. Jeffrey archer was on top of the list because he knew how to write page-turners. Jeffrey archer became an easy entry point into english fiction. His books were what you read after the homework was done.

Article Title: ‘So many have faded out’: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi cautioned with Vinod Kambli example

Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has already generated enormous excitement around Indian cricket , but former India captain Kapil Dev believes it is far too early to judge whether the teenage sensation can go on to become the next big name in the game.At 15, Sooryavanshi has already made a significant impact at the age-group, India A, IPL and is now part of India’s T20I setup. But with the youngster currently waiting for his opportunity behind the established opening pair of Abhishek Sharma and Sanju Samson, Kapil believes there is little value in rushing to make predictions about his future.“It’s too early. Does he have the ability? Yes. But there have been so many in cricket who came with so much ability, then faded out,” Kapil told Times of India.Kapil cited former India batter Vinod Kambli as an example of a player whose immense talent did not translate into the kind of long-term career many expected.“Look at Vinod Kambli. What we will say about that?” he said.Sooryavanshi, who is still only 15, has plenty of time on his side. Kapil believes the next few years will be more revealing than his current performances.“Vaibhav is 15 years old. Give him another three years, then we will talk.When his lifestyle changes, his thinking too will change. Then we’ll come to know how he will look after the next two years. That is more important than looking at his performance,” Kapil said.The teenager has already given Indian cricket plenty to talk about. In June, in his last innings as an uncapped player, Sooryavanshi smashed the fastest fifty in List A cricket, reaching the milestone in just 11 balls before finishing with 94 off 29 balls for India A in the tri-series final against Sri Lanka A.Earlier in February, he produced another remarkable performance in the Under-19 World Cup final in Harare, smashing 175 off 80 balls to help India Under-19 win the title. His IPL career also began with a bang, In 2026 season he broke several batting records this year and won the Orange Cap before being blooded into India’s T20I side.But Kapil’s broader view of young cricketers is not about one innings or one season. He said he is always looking for players who can potentially stay at the top level for a decade or more.“Any young cricketer who we can feel has a future for the next 10 years, 15 years. Those type of cricketers. We have seen Rohit, Virat. We already saw Sachin. And they made us so proud,” Kapil told Times of India.“But you’re always looking for the next hero. You always ask, ‘Who is the next hero?’ As a cricketer I like to see which is that young boy who has got that chance, who can replace Virat Kohli . And play for 15 years. That’s what my mind looks for.”For Sooryavanshi, the attention is unlikely to disappear anytime soon. But Kapil’s message is clear: talent can open the door, but how a teenager develops away from the spotlight may ultimately determine how long he stays at the top.
Article Summary: Vaibhav sooryavanshi has already made a significant impact at the age-group, india a, ipl and is now part of india’s t20i setup. Former india captain kapil dev believes it is far too early to judge whether the teenage sensation can go on to become the next big name in the game.

Why Srikkanth wants Impact Player rule removed

'I am working just as hard on my bowling'

Naman Dhir made a strong statement on his T20I debut against the West Indies, and his performance has already led to questions about Washington Sundar ’s place in India’s white-ball teams.The 25-year-old, who has mainly been seen as a batting all-rounder in the IPL, surprised many with the ball in the first T20I. He bowled his full four-over spell and returned figures of 3/31 as India restricted the West Indies to 171.Dhir had scored 318 runs in IPL 2026 but did not bowl a single over during the tournament. His international debut showed that he can offer India another option with the ball.Former India cricketer and 1983 World Cup winner Krishnamachari Srikkanth believes Dhir’s emergence could seriously hurt Washington Sundar’s chances in white-ball cricket.Srikkanth pointed out that Dhir initially came into the team as a replacement but has now made it difficult for the selectors to leave him out."Naman Dhir has now come in at Washington Sundar's place as a replacement player. Washington Sundar keeps getting injured after every two matches. Now Naman Dhir has come in as his replacement and finished him. How can you drop Naman Dhir now from ODIs and T20Is? He has immediately grabbed that spot.Now Washington Sundar can only play for India in Test cricket," Srikkanth said on his YouTube channel.Srikkanth was also impressed by how Dhir adjusted his bowling after getting hit."When he bowls fast, he gets hit for sixes. So he immediately slows the ball down, which shows that he's a very thoughtful bowler. He's ideal for T20 cricket. He bowls in such a way that he envisions himself batting and how one would bowl to him. That's how much of a thinking cricketer he looks to be. That's why he's an intelligent bowler."Dhir’s performance also made Srikkanth question the impact of the IPL’s Impact Player rule."This is why the Impact Player rule should be removed in the IPL. That's how you'll produce genuine all-rounders. Now you've got a good batting all-rounder in Naman Dhir. Today he bowled four overs, but even if he gives you two overs on a consistent basis, it'll be huge for India and MI," said Srikkanth.Srikkanth expects Dhir to get more opportunities with the ball in the IPL as well."He'll take loads of wickets even in the upcoming IPL. He must have bowled only 10 overs maximum in his IPL career, yet he bowled four overs today. He has everything, including luck."Dhir, however, made it clear that his bowling was not something he suddenly picked up for his international debut.“I have been bowling for quite some time; it is not as if I have just started now. In the IPL, because of the impact-player rule, you don’t see me bowling as much. But it is not that I haven’t bowled. I have bowled a lot and have good experience here as well. Hopefully, I will continue doing well in the future,” Dhir said in the post-match press conference after helping India bowl out West Indies for 171 in the first T20I here.He explained that he followed a simple plan after watching Axar Patel bowl earlier in the innings.“I saw Axar Bhai bowling earlier, and he was bowling a little slower and getting some turn. That was in my mind - if I bowled a little slower, there would be good grip from the wicket, and I could get them out. So I just stuck to my plans and kept things basic. I think I got a good result from that," Dhir said.Dhir also stressed that his bowling has always received the same attention as his batting.“Again, I will say that even if you haven’t seen me bowling, I have been bowling as much as I have since I came here and I have practised just as much before this. It is not as if, as a batting all-rounder or bowling all-rounder, I have neglected one aspect. Yes, my batting is a plus point, but at the same time I am working just as hard on my bowling,” he said.“Whether I have to bowl four overs, two overs or even one-day cricket, where I have bowled six or seven overs, it is normal for me. I just have to focus on my plans and try to execute them,” he added.India, who won the three-match ODI series 2-1, are leading the five-match T20I series 1-0.The second T20I match will be playd on Friday at the JSCA International Stadium Complex in Ranchi.

The 25-year-old had scored 318 runs in ipl 2026 but did not bowl a single over during the tournament. Former india cricketer and 1983 world cup winner krishnamachari srikkanth believes dhir’s emergence could seriously hurt washington sundar's chances in white-ball cricket.

Article Title: Why did Jon Rahm quit LIV Golf? Reason behind $300 million star’s departure explained
Article Text:
Jon Rahm quits LIV Golf. Image via: Richard Heathcote/ Getty Images

Why did Jon Rahm quit LIV Golf?

What does Rahm's exit mean for LIV Golf and his next move?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Jon Rahm is leaving LIV Golf. His lawyer, John Beck, told a New Jersey bankruptcy judge on Wednesday that the Spaniard reviewed the terms of the league's restructured version, called LIV 2.0, and found them unacceptable. Rahm signed in December 2023 and has won the league's season title three years running. The two-time major champion won't be part of the rebuilt tour, and both sides are working on a separation agreement. Money looks like the core issue, though neither has spelled out the terms.Jon Rahm signed as the reigning Masters champion on a deal reported at more than $300 million. He won four LIV events, but the paychecks are where the trouble sits. LIV filed for Chapter 11 protection on Sept. 8, listing between $500 million and $1 billion in liabilities. Rahm tops the league's list of 30 largest unsecured claims at $7.5 million in past-due payments. He had also said he had no regrets about joining and wanted the league to be sustainable.The second version of the league looks nothing like the first. CEO Scott O'Neil has described 10 events with smaller purses, and said the league has to move away from a Saudi-style plan toward one that stands on its own.A proposed $300 million investment from BC Partners depends on conditions that include new player agreements. Nobody is forced to sign one. Players have no obligation to join LIV 2.0, even with multiyear deals on the books.Beck told the court the terms were "unacceptable as to him." No figures came with the statement. In May, Rahm had said he saw few ways out of a contract with several years left. The bankruptcy has since changed his circumstances, and it was later said both camps are in advanced talks on a consensual separation.The PGA Tour door looks shut. CEO Brian Rolapp said on Sept. 15 that the tour has no plans to bring back the Returning Member Program, the route Brooks Koepka used to rejoin. Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau and Cameron Smith were the other names it could have covered.The DP World Tour is the other path. Rahm settled his dispute with the European circuit in May, which kept his membership and his Ryder Cup eligibility for next year. Where he plays in 2027 is not settled.The $300 million star has a thin major record since the move. He has one top-five and four top-10 finishes at majors, after three top-10s in 2023 alone.LIV has its own problems. Sergio Garcia has been released from his contract, and the deadline for current players to commit now sits at Oct. 25. It is not clear which players BC Partners requires for the deal to close, so Rahm's absence adds to the uncertainty. Following his departure, DeChambeau is the biggest name left on the roster.
Article Summary: Masters champion jon rahm is leaving liv golf. The two-time major champion won't be part of the rebuilt tour. Both sides are working on a separation agreement. Liv filed for chapter 11 protection on sept. 8, listing between $500 million and $1 billion in liabilities.

Article Title: Candace Parker finally reveals Caitlin Clark’s heated playoff moment after the Fever star screamed at the WNBA legend
Article Text:
Caitlin Clark. Image via: Trevor Ruszkowski-Imagn Images

What did Caitlin Clark yell at Candace Parker?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

How much did WNBA playoff viewership drop after the Fever lost?

Caitlin Clark hit a big three against the Aces, turned toward the scorer's table, and screamed at Candace Parker. The WNBA legend was sitting there minding her own business. Parker has now explained what she heard, and the answer includes a pointed question and one swear word that cannot be printed here. She went through it on Wednesday's Post Moves podcast, which she co-hosts with Clark's Fever teammate Aaliyah Boston, and kept things light with a Steph Curry comparison. Las Vegas won the first-round series 2-1 and eliminated the Fever.Candace Parker was telling the story to Aaliyah Boston. She was at the scorer's table, she said, when Clark knocked down the three and turned on her. Parker was unsure of the exact words, so she tried two versions out loud. Did Clark ask what she thought this was, or did a curse word sit in the middle of the question?Parker went with the second. Boston, laughing, confirmed it. Parker's own reaction was simple. She wanted to say great shot, keep things moving, and go back to sitting there.The pair had already settled it in person. After the game, cameras appeared to catch the Fever point guard telling Parker, "I blacked out," and both laughed it off.Parker gave the moment some context. She pointed to a night years ago when Curry hit a shot and walked over to Reggie Miller, who was calling the game, to say something.Same energy, she said, and she found it cool. The three-time Finals champion added that she wanted opponents to do exactly this when she played. She asked for the trash talk and the finger in her face because it fired her up. Some players feed off chaos, in Parker's view, and she used to be one of them.Her verdict on Clark's outburst was short.The Fever's exit set off a ratings argument almost right away. A post on X claimed the playoffs lost 70 to 76 percent of their viewers once Clark was gone. It had no source and passed a million views in about 18 hours. Other accounts pushed the figure as high as 78 percent.The fairer comparison is Game 1 of Fever-Aces against the two Game 1s of the semifinals, played Sunday. USA Today reporter Christine Brennan posted the numbers: 2.11 million viewers for Fever-Aces on ABC, 1.17 million for Liberty-Dream on ABC, and 1.12 million for Aces-Valkyries on NBC and Peacock. Front Office Sports reporter Colin Salao shared the same figures. By that math, the drop is 44 to 47 percent.It is still a big fall, but it is well short of the viral claims. Each semifinal opener still pulled more than a million viewers, and four teams are chasing the title.
Article Summary: Caitlin clark hit a big three against the aces, turned toward the scorer's table, and screamed at candace parker. Parker has now explained what she heard, and the answer includes a pointed question and one swear word that cannot be printed here. The pair had already settled it in person.

Randi Mahomes found another way to use her connection with Kansas City sports to help children. Article Title: Two runners completed the London Marathon inside one giant inflatable elephant in 4:15:40; they set a world record while raising money for type 1 diabetes
Article Text:
PC: Cornish Times

How did two runners set a marathon world record in an inflatable elephant

The teamwork behind the inflatable elephant marathon

How did Jo turn a failed lobster attempt into an elephant world record

The elephant costume turned a marathon into a memorable challenge

Two runners from Looe have set a world record after completing the London Marathon inside a giant inflatable elephant. Jo Robinson and Emma Langstaff finished the race in 4:15:40, recording the fastest marathon time ever recorded in a two-person inflatable costume. As members of the Looe Pioneers running club, they took on the challenge to raise money and awareness for type one diabetes.According to the Cornish Times, Emma works as a doctor and treats patients with type one diabetes, while both of Jo’s daughters live with type one diabetes. The pair had trained only twice in the costume before race day, but worked together to manage shorter steps and a matching cadence. Their run also followed Jo’s failed attempt to set a record dressed as a lobster in 2023.Jo Robinson and Emma Langstaff completed the London Marathon in 4:15:40 while wearing an inflatable elephant costume. The time they took to run the marathon made them the fastest pair ever to complete one in a two-person inflatable costume.They are members of the Looe Pioneers running club, but the challenge was about more than the novelty of running as an elephant. They also wanted to raise money and awareness for type one diabetes.Emma is a doctor who works with patients living with the condition. Both of Jo’s daughters are also suffering from type one diabetes. Jo said, “It was physically demanding, especially starting further back, but we spent much of the race overtaking people, which gave us a real lift psychologically. I’m not sure those being passed by an elephant enjoyed it quite as much, but it certainly kept us going.”The shared inflatable costume meant the pair had to change their usual running style. Jo Robinson said, “You’ve got to completely change your stride”“Shorter steps, matching cadence, it’s all about working together. But I knew Emma was the perfect partner. We’ve done loads together over the years.”“We only practised twice, once along Hannafore in the dark and once around town on a Saturday night”“I think we definitely confused a few people who were out as there were some faces like, ‘I need to stop drinking!”The elephant challenge also had a personal significance for Jo Robinson. In 2023, she made an attempt at a Guinness World Record while dressed as a lobster, but the effort ended in failure when the costume became soaked.Jo said, “The costume got soaked and it was like running with a wet towel wrapped round my legs”.“This time, I was determined to get it done.”The London Marathon also left a strong impression on the runners. Jo had previously taken part in the Paris and Berlin marathons, but said neither compared with London because of the crowd support. She said the cheers from strangers gave the runners a boost and kept them going throughout the race.The Cornish Times reports they now have a certificate of sorts, but the official one still needs to be ordered. Both runners are turning 50 this year, but said their plans were not the result of a midlife crisis. Instead, they said their motivation came from their love of running, sense of humour and desire to do something different.They are already considering their next challenges, including the Scilly 60 and the New York Marathon. Jo said the elephant made people smile, which was what the challenge was all about. The record attempt brought together their running experience, their efforts to raise money and awareness for type one diabetes, and a memorable sight for marathon spectators.
Article Summary: Jo robinson and emma langstaff completed the london marathon in 4:15:40. It is the fastest marathon time ever recorded in a two-person inflatable costume. The pair are members of the looe pioneers running club. They wanted to raise money and awareness for type one diabetes.

Sebastian Burley, 36, finished the 26.2-mile course in 4:00:33 on Sunday, 26 April 2026, becoming the fastest man to complete a marathon in a full-body inflatable costume, according to Guinness World Records . Guinness says 38 record titles were set or broken during the marathon, with 39 record holders. The records covered a wide range of categories, including costume-based attempts and challenges involving different types of clothing and equipment.Burley's record appears on Guinness's official record page as the fastest marathon in a full-body inflatable costume by a male, with a time of 4:00:33. The record was achieved at the TCS London Marathon in London on 26 April 2026. Other 2026 record holders included Keyur Gudka, who ran the marathon in traditional Indian dress in 3:08:10, Simon Fannon, who knitted a 5.59-metre scarf while running in 5:48:08, and Sabastian Sawe, who set the men's marathon record with a time of 1:59:30.The 2026 list also included records for runners dressed as a three-dimensional toy, a firefighter, a camera, a clown, an electrical engineer and a sweet food, among other categories. Guinness says the London Marathon has worked with the organisation for almost 2 decades, giving runners the opportunity to attempt records while also supporting fundraising efforts.Burley’s 4:00:33 translates to approximately 9 minutes 10 seconds per mile, or about 5 minutes 42 seconds per kilometre. A pre-race listing identified Arnie Delstanche as the record holder with a time of 4:07:46, meaning Burley’s finish was 7 minutes and 13 seconds faster. The physical challenge was not simply the distance. Before the marathon, Burley had described the inflatable chicken costume as becoming extremely hot and humid inside. He also said that running in windy conditions felt like running with a parachute. He had previously run in the chicken costume and was preparing to attempt the record while raising money for Action for Children. The Department for Work and Pensions stresses that these are projections under specific policy and economic assumptions, rather than forecasts of what will necessarily happen. For Burley, the marathon combined a demanding physical challenge with his fundraising goal. The ball will skid on nicely, but looks an excellent pitch for batting," reckon Ajit Agarkar in 2023.Three years later, as India return to Ranchi for another T20I, Agarkar’s tenure as chairman of selectors has come to an end.The BCCI invited applications on Tuesday to fill the vacant position in the men’s selection committee following Agarkar’s exit. Agarkar’s tenure ended on October 4. The former India pacer had informed the board after its Annual General Meeting on September 18 that he would not seek an extension.Pragyan Ojha is currently the interim chairman of selectors, with Shiv Sundar Das, Ajay Ratra and RP Singh the other members of the panel.“The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) invites applications for one position on its Men's Selection Committee," the BCCI said on its website.The deadline for applications is October 14.Agarkar leaves the post after a successful period for Indian cricket. During his tenure, India won the 2024 and 2026 T20 World Cups and the 2025 Champions Trophy. The team also won two Asia Cup titles and back-to-back Asian Games gold medals, while reaching the 2023 ODI World Cup final.His tenure also saw the beginning of a major transition in Indian cricket, with Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma retiring from T20Is and Tests.The BCCI thanked Agarkar for his contribution and highlighted the major achievements during his time as chairman.“A tenure marked by some truly special moments for Indian cricket — three ICC trophies, two Asia Cup titles and back-to-back Asian Games Gold medals, along with a run to the 2023 ODI World Cup final,” the BCCI posted on its official X account.“Thank you, Mr Ajit Agarkar for your commitment, conviction and contribution as Chairman of the Men’s Selection Committee. Wishing you the very best for the journey ahead,” the board added.

Article Title: ‘History that will last forever’: Cristiano Ronaldo pays tribute to Lionel Messi with ‘utmost respect’

Ronaldo’s message to Lionel Messi after international retirement

Cristiano Ronaldo put aside one of football’s most enduring rivalries to pay tribute to Lionel Messi after the Argentine bid an emotional farewell to international football.Messi, 39, made his final appearance for Argentina on Tuesday, signing off in style as he scored once and created two goals in a 3-0 friendly victory over Benin at Buenos Aires’ Monumental Stadium. More than 85,000 fans were present as Argentina celebrated the end of his remarkable 21-year international career.Following the match, Messi took to Instagram to reflect on his journey with the national team and admitted that he was already missing the feeling of representing Argentina in the famous blue and white shirt."Yesterday was my last game, and I already miss wearing the blue and white. I know I'm making the right decision," Messi said in a lengthy Instagram post. "It's been an incredible journey, full of joy and also some sadness, but I know for sure that every step I took was worth it..."I don't want to forget Diego (Maradona), who put our country where it deserved to be and who, as I always say, I know helped us both by being here with us and also from heaven, with every step we took."Thank you to the clubs where I played, for always respecting my feelings and allowing me to dedicate myself to my country whenever it was time to put on the national team jersey..."Messi's international career included Argentina's 2022 World Cup triumph, Copa America titles in 2021 and 2024, and victory in the 2022 Finalissima."I am grateful. I love you all very much; I'm going to miss you, and I will always thank you for having been by our side, by my side," the Inter Miami playmaker added.Among those to respond to Messi's farewell message was Ronaldo, his long-time rival in the debate over the greatest player of their generation. Despite their careers being defined by competition for individual and team honours, the Portugal captain offered a warm tribute to the Argentine."Leo, after so many years of defending your country, you've made history that will last forever. I have the utmost respect for what you've accomplished with Argentina. A hug," Ronaldo said.Ronaldo, 41, has himself been in the spotlight with Portugal after becoming embroiled in a dispute with coach Jorge Jesus following his abrupt departure from the national team's training camp.For Messi, however, the international chapter ended with a memorable night in front of a packed Monumental, bringing an emotional close to more than two decades of representing Argentina.

Article Title: ‘Play more cricket’: Kapil Dev’s blunt take on Hardik Pandya’s injury woes

Hardik Pandya’s prolonged absence from competitive cricket has once again brought the issue of player workload, game time and injuries into focus, with India also dealing with fitness concerns involving several other players.Pandya has not played competitive cricket since the final week of IPL 2026. He was expected to return for India A in the upcoming ODI series against Australia A, beginning October 6, but his comeback was delayed. He is now ruled out of the upcoming white-ball tour of New Zealand.So what does Pandya need to do to be available more often?“Play more cricket,” former India captain Kapil Dev told Times of India.Asked if he felt Pandya was not doing that, Kapil said: “I don’t know. You play more, your body gets tuned to that. But if you play less and suddenly you play more, chances of injury increase. If your muscles are fine, your injuries are less.”Kapil’s comments come at a time when India are dealing with a number of injury concerns. Prasidh Krishna has been ruled out for at least three weeks and is highly likely to miss the upcoming five-match ODI series against New Zealand. India’s tour of New Zealand begins with the T20I series on October 22.Harshit Rana has also suffered a fitness setback and is unlikely to be picked for India’s upcoming tour of New Zealand. Rana was ruled out of the three-match T20I series against Afghanistan as well as the 2026 Asian Games last month due to injury. He was recovering at the BCCI’s Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru but developed low-grade pain in his left quadriceps during a match simulation.Pandya, meanwhile, has been away from competitive cricket since the conclusion of IPL 2026, while Harshit last featured during India’s white-ball leg against England in July.The wider spread of cricket injuries over the last four-five years also prompted a discussion with Kapil on whether the volume of cricket has contributed to the problem.The former India captain pointed to the difference in the playing patterns of his generation, citing Sandeep Patil’s observation about how players used to remain involved in different forms of domestic cricket.“Sandeep Patil put it very nicely. ‘In our time we used to play Ranji Trophy , Duleep Trophy, club cricket, other cricket too.’ In 365 days, if you can play 250 days, you’re in the game.”For Kapil, regular cricket helps the body stay accustomed to the demands of the game. For India, Pandya’s prolonged absence and the fitness concerns surrounding several other players underline the challenge of keeping key players available for longer stretches.

He was expected to return for india a in the upcoming odi series against australia a, beginning october 6, but his comeback was delayed. Pandya is now ruled out of the upcoming white-ball tour of new zealand.
